2018A16.goal: From the right-angle vertex $B$ of a $20$-$21$ right triangle we draw segments to points on the hypotenuse $AC$. As the endpoint slides from $A$ to $C$, the length changes continuously; we count how many integer lengths occur, counting each segment separately.

tools.name: Altitude to the hypotenuse
tools.why: Area two ways: $\tfrac12\cdot20\cdot21=\tfrac12\cdot29\cdot h$.

tools.name: Intermediate value idea
tools.fact: \text{A continuously changing length hits every value between its extremes.}
tools.why: As the endpoint moves from $A$ to the foot of the altitude, the length falls from $20$ to $h$; then it rises to $21$.

2018A16.approach: The shortest segment is the altitude. Going from $A$ to the foot, lengths decrease from $20$ to $h$, hitting each value in between once; from the foot to $C$ they increase from $h$ to $21$. Count integers in each range separately and add.

steps.title: Find the altitude
steps.explain: $AC=29$ and $h=\tfrac{20\cdot21}{29}=\tfrac{420}{29}\approx14.48$. Since $h$ is not an integer, no integer length occurs exactly at the foot.

check.q: For a $6$-$8$-$10$ right triangle, what is the altitude to the hypotenuse?

steps.title: Count on each side
steps.explain: From $A$ to the foot: integer lengths $15,16,\ldots,20$, that is $6$ segments. From the foot to $C$: $15,16,\ldots,21$, that is $7$ segments. Each length below $20$ appears once on each side.

steps.title: Add
steps.explain: $6+7=13$ segments, including $BA=20$ and $BC=21$.

2018A16.bridge: Find the altitude, then count integer lengths on each side of its foot.
solution: Lengths from $B$ decrease from $20$ to $14.48$ along $A\to$ foot, giving integers $15$–$20$: $6$.
They increase from $14.48$ to $21$ along foot $\to C$, giving integers $15$–$21$: $7$.
traps: Counting each length once instead of once per side.
Starting the count at $14$ (the altitude is greater than $14$).
2018A16.recognize: Distances from a point to points on a segment: the minimum is the perpendicular distance, and values between the min and each endpoint are hit once on each side.

2018A17.goal: We choose $6$ numbers from $1$ to $12$ so that no chosen number divides another. We want the smallest possible least element. Organising numbers by their odd part reveals forced choices.

tools.name: Chains by odd part
tools.why: Every number is $2^k\times(\text{odd})$; within a chain each divides the next.

tools.name: Pigeonhole
tools.why: Two numbers from the same chain would divide each other.

2018A17.approach: Split $\{1,\ldots,12\}$ into $6$ chains by odd part. Since two numbers in a chain divide each other, we take exactly one from each chain. That forces $7,9,11$, and $9$ then rules out $3$, and so on. Push the smallest element as low as these forced choices allow, and give an example.

steps.title: One from each chain
steps.explain: The six chains are listed above. We must pick one number from each, so $7$, $9$ and $11$ are in the set.

steps.title: Rule out small values
steps.explain: $3$ divides $9$, so from $\{3,6,12\}$ we take $6$ or $12$, both even. $1$ divides everything. $2$ divides $6$ and $12$, so $2$ is impossible. So the least element is at least $4$.

check.q: Why can't $3$ be in the set?

steps.title: An example with $4$
steps.explain: $\{4,5,6,7,9,11\}$: no element divides another ($4\nmid6$, $5,6,7$ are fine, $9$ and $11$ have no divisors in the set). So $4$ is achievable.

2018A17.bridge: Use the six odd-part chains, apply the forced choices, and test the smallest candidate.
solution: $9$ is forced, so not $3$; the $3$-chain gives $6$ or $12$, so not $2$; and not $1$.
The least element can be $4$. The answer is $\textbf{(C)}\ 4$.
2018A17.shortcut: Write each number as $2^k\cdot\text{odd}$; the number of chains equals the maximum size of a divisor-free set.
traps: Choosing $3$ without noticing $9$ is forced.
Forgetting $1$ divides everything.
2018A17.recognize: "No element divides another" problems: group numbers into chains by odd part (or by repeated doubling); a set can contain at most one from each chain.

2018A18.goal: We count nonnegative integers of the form $\sum_{i=0}^7a_i3^i$ with each $a_i\in\{-1,0,1\}$. This is "balanced ternary" with $8$ digits.

tools.name: Balanced ternary
tools.fact: \text{Every integer in }\left[-\tfrac{3^8-1}2,\tfrac{3^8-1}2\right]\text{ has exactly one 8-digit representation}
tools.why: Add $\sum3^i$ to shift digits $\{-1,0,1\}$ to $\{0,1,2\}$; ordinary base $3$ is unique.

tools.name: Geometric sum
tools.why: Sum of a geometric series.

2018A18.approach: Shift each digit up by $1$: $a_i+1\in\{0,1,2\}$, which is ordinary base $3$. So the values are exactly the integers from $-3280$ to $3280$, each once. Count the nonnegative ones.

steps.title: Shift to ordinary base 3
steps.explain: $\sum a_i3^i=\sum(a_i+1)3^i-\sum3^i$. As $a_i+1$ ranges over $\{0,1,2\}$, $\sum(a_i+1)3^i$ takes each value $0,\ldots,3^8-1$ exactly once. Subtracting $3280$ gives every integer from $-3280$ to $3280$.

check.q: With $2$ balanced ternary digits, which integers can you make?

steps.title: Count nonnegative values
steps.explain: From $0$ to $3280$: $3281$ integers.

2018A18.bridge: Shift the digits to ordinary base $3$ and count the nonnegative values.
solution: Shifting digits by $1$ turns the form into base $3$, minus $\sum3^i=3280$.
So the representable numbers are exactly $-3280,\ldots,3280$.
2018A18.shortcut: By symmetry ($a_i\to-a_i$), half of the $3^8=6561$ values are negative, half positive, plus $0$: $\tfrac{6561+1}2=3281$.
traps: Answering $3^8=6561$ (that counts all values, including negatives).
Forgetting $0$.
2018A18.recognize: Digits from $\{-1,0,1\}$: balanced ternary. Shifting digits by a constant converts to an ordinary base.

2018A19.goal: $m$ is chosen from $\{11,13,15,17,19\}$ and $n$ from $1999$ to $2018$ ($20$ values). We want $P(m^n\text{ ends in }1)$. Only the units digit of $m$ and the cycle of its powers matter.

tools.name: Units digit cycles
tools.why: The units digit of a power depends only on the units digit of the base and repeats in a short cycle.

2018A19.approach: For each $m$, decide which exponents make the units digit $1$, using its cycle. Count those $n$ among the $20$ and add up the favourable pairs.

steps.title: Cycles
steps.explain: $11^n$ always ends in $1$. $13^n$ and $17^n$ end in $1$ when $4\mid n$. $15^n$ never. $19^n$ ends in $1$ when $n$ is even.

check.q: What is the units digit of $7^{8}$?
How many multiples of $4$ are in $1999,\ldots,2018$?

2018A19.bridge: Use units-digit cycles to count favourable $n$ for each $m$.
traps: Using $n\bmod4$ for $19$ instead of $n\bmod2$.
Counting $19$ values of $n$ instead of $20$.
2018A19.recognize: Units digits of large powers: use the cycle of the base's last digit.

2018A20.goal: A $7\times7$ grid coloured black and white must look the same under all rotations by $90^\circ$ and all four reflections, and must use both colours. We count such colourings. Cells that are mapped to each other must share a colour.

tools.name: Orbits of cells
tools.why: Each group of cells that symmetries move into each other must be one colour; different groups are independent.

tools.name: Fundamental triangle
tools.why: Each orbit has exactly one cell in the triangular eighth of the grid between the centre, a side midpoint and a corner.

2018A20.approach: The symmetries divide the $49$ cells into classes. Pick one representative of each class: a triangular wedge (one eighth of the square) does this. Count its cells, raise $2$ to that power, and remove the two one-colour grids.

steps.title: Find the classes
steps.explain: Consider the wedge from the centre to the middle of the top edge to the top-right corner. Going outward from the centre, its rows contain $1,2,3,4$ cells: $10$ cells. Every cell of the grid is a rotation or reflection of exactly one of these.

check.q: How many classes does a $3\times3$ grid have under the same symmetries?

steps.title: Count colourings
steps.explain: Each class can be black or white independently: $2^{10}=1024$. Remove all-black and all-white: $1022$.

2018A20.bridge: Count the cell classes under the symmetries, then use $2^{\text{classes}}-2$.
solution: Symmetric colourings are constant on each class of cells moved into each other by the $8$ symmetries.
A one-eighth wedge contains one cell of each class: $1+2+3+4=10$ classes.
$2^{10}=1024$ symmetric colourings, minus the $2$ single-colour ones.
2018A20.shortcut: For an odd $n=2k+1$ grid with full square symmetry, the classes number $\tfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}2$.
traps: Forgetting to subtract the two one-colour codes.
Using only rotations (that gives more classes).
2018A20.recognize: Colourings invariant under symmetries: count orbits (classes) of cells; each orbit is coloured independently.

2018A21.goal: We want all $a$ for which the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$ and the parabola $y=x^2-a$ meet in exactly $3$ points. Eliminate $x^2$ to get an equation in $y$ alone, then count the points each solution gives.

tools.name: Substitution
tools.why: Replace $x^2$ in the circle equation.

tools.name: Factoring
tools.why: Expand: $y^2+y-ay+ay+a-a^2$.

tools.name: Points from a $y$-value
tools.why: Each $y$ gives $x=\pm\sqrt{y+a}$.

2018A21.approach: Substitute $x^2=y+a$ into the circle to get a quadratic in $y$, which factors. Each root $y$ gives $0$, $1$ or $2$ points depending on $y+a$. Three points means one root gives $1$ point and the other gives $2$.

steps.title: Points from each root
steps.explain: $y=-a$ gives $x^2=0$: one point $(0,-a)$. $y=a-1$ gives $x^2=2a-1$: two points if $a>\tfrac12$. The roots must differ ($a\ne\tfrac12$).

check.q: For $a=1$, how many points does $y=a-1$ give?

steps.title: Conclude
steps.explain: Exactly $3$ points exactly when $a>\tfrac12$.

check.q: At $a=\tfrac12$, how many intersection points are there?

2018A21.bridge: Eliminate $x^2$, factor the quadratic in $y$, and count points from each root.
solution: $y=a-1$ gives $x^2=2a-1$: two more points exactly when $a>\tfrac12$.
So exactly $3$ points iff $a>\tfrac12$. The answer is $\textbf{(E)}$.
2018A21.shortcut: Sketch: the parabola's vertex $(0,-a)$ is always on the circle; it crosses the circle twice more only if it opens wide enough, $a>\tfrac12$.
traps: Solving for $x$ first and getting a quartic.
Forgetting the tangent point at $x=0$ counts once.
2018A21.recognize: Intersections of a circle and a parabola $y=x^2+\ldots$: substitute $x^2$ to get a quadratic in $y$, then convert each $y$-root into $0$, $1$ or $2$ points.

2018A22.goal: Four positive integers have given pairwise gcds around a cycle, and $\gcd(d,a)$ is between $70$ and $100$. We want a prime that must divide $a$. Track the exact powers of $2$ and $3$ in each number.

tools.name: gcd via exponents
tools.why: The gcd takes the smaller power of each prime.

tools.name: Factorisations
tools.why: Reading the gcds as exponent constraints.

2018A22.approach: Work prime by prime. From the three known gcds, determine the exact $2$-adic and $3$-adic valuations needed for $a$ and $d$. Then $\gcd(d,a)=2^?3^?\cdot k$ with $k$ coprime to $6$, and the range $70$–$100$ pins $k$ down.

steps.title: Powers of 3
steps.explain: $\gcd(b,c)=36$ has $3^2$, but $c$ also has $3^3$ (from $\gcd(c,d)=54$), so $v_3(b)=2$. Then $\gcd(a,b)=24$ has $3^1$ with $v_3(b)=2$, so $v_3(a)=1$. Since $v_3(d)\ge3$: $v_3(\gcd(d,a))=1$.

steps.title: Powers of 2
steps.explain: $24\mid b$ gives $v_2(b)\ge3$, so $\gcd(b,c)=36$ forces $v_2(c)=2$. Then $\gcd(c,d)=54$ (one $2$) forces $v_2(d)=1$. And $v_2(a)\ge3$. So $v_2(\gcd(d,a))=1$.

steps.title: Pin down the gcd
steps.explain: So $\gcd(d,a)=6k$ with $k$ coprime to $6$. $70<6k<100$ gives $k\in\{12,\ldots,16\}$, and only $k=13$ is coprime to $6$. So $13\mid a$.

check.why: The others are divisible by $2$ or $3$.

2018A22.bridge: Track $v_2$ and $v_3$ around the cycle, then use the range for $\gcd(d,a)$.
2018A22.shortcut: Once you know $\gcd(d,a)=6\times(\text{coprime to }6)$, check $72,78,84,90,96$: only $78=6\cdot13$ works.
traps: Assuming $\gcd(d,a)$ is a multiple of $24$ or $54$.
Choosing $k=15$ (it shares the factor $3$).
2018A22.recognize: Chains of gcd conditions: go prime by prime with valuations; each gcd fixes a minimum, which often forces exact exponents.

2018A23.goal: A $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle has a square $S$ in its right-angle corner, and the square's far corner is $2$ units from the hypotenuse. We need the planted fraction, i.e. $1-\tfrac{\text{area of }S}{6}$.

tools.name: Distance from a point to a line
tools.why: The standard formula from projecting onto the line's normal.

tools.name: Hypotenuse as a line
tools.why: It passes through $(4,0)$ and $(0,3)$.

2018A23.approach: Put the right angle at the origin with legs along the axes. The square has side $s$ and far corner $(s,s)$, which is the point of the square closest to the hypotenuse. Set its distance to the hypotenuse equal to $2$ and solve for $s$.

steps.title: Coordinates
steps.explain: Legs: $x$ from $0$ to $4$, $y$ from $0$ to $3$. Hypotenuse: $3x+4y=12$. The square is $[0,s]\times[0,s]$, closest to the hypotenuse at $(s,s)$.

steps.title: Distance equals 2
steps.explain: $\tfrac{12-7s}{5}=2$, so $7s=2$ and $s=\tfrac27$. The square's area is $\tfrac4{49}$.

check.q: What is the distance from $(1,1)$ to $3x+4y=12$?

2018A23.bridge: Use coordinates and the point-to-line distance from $(s,s)$ to the hypotenuse.
solution: Place the legs on the axes; the hypotenuse is $3x+4y=12$.
The square's far corner $(s,s)$ is at distance $\tfrac{12-7s}{5}=2$, so $s=\tfrac27$.
The square's area is $\tfrac4{49}$ out of $6$.
2018A23.shortcut: Distance from the origin to the hypotenuse is $\tfrac{12}5$; moving the corner to $(s,s)$ reduces it by $\tfrac{7s}{5}$.
traps: Measuring distance along a leg instead of perpendicular to the hypotenuse.
Forgetting to divide by $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$.
2018A23.recognize: "Shortest distance to a line" with right angles: set up coordinates and use the point-to-line distance formula.

2018A24.goal: In triangle $ABC$ ($AB=50$, $AC=10$, area $120$), $D,E$ are midpoints of $AB,AC$, and the angle bisector from $A$ meets $DE$ at $F$ and $BC$ at $G$. We want the area of $FDBG$. Combine the angle bisector ratio with the midline.

tools.name: Angle bisector theorem
tools.why: The bisector splits the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides.

tools.name: Triangles with the same height
tools.why: They share the height from $A$.

tools.name: Midline
tools.fact: DE\parallel BC,\ \ \triangle ADF\sim\triangle ABG\text{ with ratio }\tfrac12
tools.why: $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $DF\parallel BG$.

2018A24.approach: Quadrilateral $FDBG$ is triangle $ABG$ minus the small triangle $ADF$. The bisector theorem gives $[ABG]$, and the midline makes $ADF$ a half-scale copy of $ABG$.

steps.title: Area of $ABG$
steps.explain: $BG:GC=50:10=5:1$, so $BG=\tfrac56BC$ and $[ABG]=\tfrac56\cdot120=100$.

check.q: If $AB=6$ and $AC=3$, what fraction of $BC$ is $BG$?

steps.title: Area of $ADF$
steps.explain: $DE\parallel BC$, so $\triangle ADF\sim\triangle ABG$ with ratio $AD:AB=\tfrac12$. Areas scale by $\tfrac14$: $[ADF]=25$.

check.q: Similar triangles with side ratio $\tfrac12$ have area ratio?

2018A24.bridge: Get $[ABG]$ from the bisector theorem and subtract the half-scale triangle $ADF$.
solution: By the angle bisector theorem $BG:GC=5:1$, so $[ABG]=\tfrac56\cdot120=100$.
$DE\parallel BC$ makes $\triangle ADF\sim\triangle ABG$ with ratio $\tfrac12$: $[ADF]=25$.
2018A24.shortcut: Ratios only: the specific side lengths matter only through $AB:AC$; the area $120$ scales everything.
traps: Using $BG:GC=AC:AB$ (reversed).
Taking the area ratio of the similar triangles as $\tfrac12$ instead of $\tfrac14$.
2018A24.recognize: Angle bisectors with midpoints: the bisector theorem splits areas; midlines create similar triangles at scale $\tfrac12$.

2018A25.goal: $A_n,B_n$ are repdigits of length $n$ (digits $a,b$) and $C_n$ is a repdigit of length $2n$ (digit $c$). We want the largest $a+b+c$ for which $C_n-B_n=A_n^2$ holds for at least two values of $n$. Write repdigits algebraically.

tools.name: Polynomial identity
tools.fact: \text{A linear equation in }x\text{ true for two values of }x\text{ holds for all }x
tools.why: So the coefficients on both sides must match.

2018A25.approach: Write all three as fractions in $x=10^n$. Divide out the common factor $\tfrac{10^n-1}{9}$ to get a linear equation in $x$. Holding for two different $n$ means it holds identically, so match coefficients.

steps.title: Translate
steps.explain: With $x=10^n$: $C_n=c\tfrac{x^2-1}{9}$, $B_n=b\tfrac{x-1}9$, $A_n^2=a^2\tfrac{(x-1)^2}{81}$. Divide the equation by $\tfrac{x-1}9$: $c(x+1)-b=\tfrac{a^2}9(x-1)$.

steps.title: Match coefficients
steps.explain: True for two values of $x$ means it is an identity: $c=\tfrac{a^2}9$ and $c-b=-\tfrac{a^2}9$, so $b=2c$ and $a=3\sqrt c$.

steps.title: Maximise
steps.explain: $c$ must be a perfect square digit with $b=2c\le9$: $c=1$ gives $(a,b,c)=(3,2,1)$, sum $6$; $c=4$ gives $(6,8,4)$, sum $18$; $c=9$ gives $b=18$, impossible. Maximum $18$.

2018A25.bridge: Write the repdigits in terms of $x=10^n$, reduce to a linear identity, and match coefficients.
solution: With $x=10^n$ the equation becomes $c(x+1)-b=\tfrac{a^2}{9}(x-1)$ after dividing by $\tfrac{x-1}9$.
Holding for two values of $n$, it is an identity: $c=\tfrac{a^2}9$, $b=2c$.
traps: Allowing $b=18$ for $c=9$.
Using $C_n$ with $n$ digits instead of $2n$.
2018A25.recognize: Repdigits and "for at least two $n$": write them as $d\tfrac{10^n-1}9$, and two values of $n$ make the relation an identity.
